query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, nanoscale Y–Hf enriched surface pre-treatment to boride components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment will enhance the in-situ formation of a strongly adherent Al2O3 scale by catalyzing its nucleation and adhesion, thereby reducing molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with standard surface conditions used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.intervention: A pre-treatment step that deposits a uniform thin coating containing minor additions of yttrium and hafnium (e.g., via sputtering or chemical deposition) on the component surface prior to immersion in molten aluminum.
generation.conditions: Under typical hot-dip aluminum plating process parameters where molten aluminum is maintained at its service temperature and the exposure durations are standard, ensuring aggressive molten-aluminum attack.
generation.structural_mediator: The Y–Hf enriched layer acts as a catalyst for the rapid and uniform formation of a protective, Al2O3-rich scale on the surface during the plating process, effectively blocking further attack by the molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The reactive rare‐earth elements promote the nucleation and adhesion of Al2O3, forming a stable oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier to limit the dissolution of the underlying boride and the penetration of molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components that receive the Y–Hf pre-treatment will show significantly lower mass loss and improved corrosion resistance (demonstrated by more coherent and less spalled oxide scales) compared to untreated boride components during and after hot-dip aluminum plating.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without the Y–Hf pre-treatment undergoing the same hot-dip aluminum-plating process.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold under standard plating conditions and for uniformly deposited Y–Hf layers. If the coating is too thick, non-uniform, or if the process conditions (temperature, immersion time) differ significantly from typical values, the beneficial effect may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: Although similar improvements have been observed in Y–Hf co-doped high-entropy alloy coatings under high-temperature corrosive conditions, specific interactions at the boride–molten aluminum interface may affect the kinetics and stability of oxide formation, and thus the precise magnitude of improvement is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of boride-based specimens: one group receives the nanoscale Y–Hf coating and the other remains untreated. Process both groups in an identical hot-dip aluminum-plating operation under standard conditions. After plating, perform corrosion tests including mass loss measurements and detailed surface analyses using SEM, EDS, and adhesion assessments of the oxide scale.
measurements: Thickness, uniformity, and composition of the oxide scale
Quantitative adhesion strength of the oxide layer
Electrochemical corrosion rate in molten aluminum-mimicking conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y–Hf pre-treated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass loss, a more uniform and adherent Al2O3 scale, and lower corrosion rates relative to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C. The mechanism for the coatings under Na2SO4 + NaCl hot corrosion is described as follows [,,,]. Initially, chlorine reacts with the metal to form metal chlorides (MClx).
